scenario.label: Asset loan cohort, first repayment cycle
scenario.brief: Eight people took an asset loan from us six months ago - a grinding machine, a freezer, a tricycle, a borehole pump. Repayment is behind across the cohort. I do not want to ask "did you repay". I want to understand what happened after they received the asset: whether the business is actually operating, what revenue it is making, what prevented repayment, what support they got from us, and whether the same thing is happening to several of them. I need to know whether this is about individual people or about how we designed the loan.
scenario.theDecision: Five of the eight share one cause: the repayment schedule starts 30 days after disbursement and every one of these assets takes two to three months to produce income. That is the lending model, not the people. Two are genuinely trading and repaying. One never took delivery of the asset at all and nobody from us noticed for six months. A right answer separates the systemic five from the individual one and says the model needs the grace period changed.

people.name: Amaka Nwachukwu
people.remit: Runs the asset finance programme. Reads what comes back and decides what changes.
people.truth: She designed the loan: repayment begins 30 days after disbursement, weekly instalments, 12 months. She has not looked at when each asset actually starts earning. She thinks the problem is selection and is considering tightening who qualifies. She does not know that one borrower never received their asset.
people.manner: Direct, data-minded, open to being wrong. Answers what she is asked.

people.name: Sunday Eze
people.truth: Received the grinder in month one. It took him ten weeks to build a customer base; he now grinds for about 40 people a week and earns roughly N45,000 a week. The first three repayments fell due before he had any customers and he missed them. He has paid every week since week 12. He is behind by the three he missed at the start.
people.manner: Calm and clear. Gives figures. Not defensive.

people.name: Hauwa Ibrahim
people.truth: Received the freezer. Sells frozen fish. Took about two months to establish supply. Now earns about N30,000 a week and is repaying. Missed the first six weeks entirely because there was no income yet. Says she told the field officer at the time and nothing changed.
people.manner: Brief and matter-of-fact. Mentions telling somebody, once, without dwelling on it.

people.name: Chinedu Obi
people.truth: Received the tricycle and it was earning within a week. Has repaid every instalment on time. Wants a second loan for a second tricycle. Nothing is wrong.
people.manner: Confident and quick. Has nothing to complain about and says so.

people.name: Blessing Ade
people.truth: The pump was installed in month two after a delay on our side. Water sales started in month three. Repayment started falling due in month one, so she is behind by eight instalments she could not possibly have paid. She is now paying weekly and has not missed one since month three.
people.manner: Polite, apologetic about arrears that are not her fault, and will say the dates if asked.

people.name: Musa Danjuma
people.truth: NEVER RECEIVED THE MACHINE. He was approved and signed, the loan was disbursed against his name, and the supplier never delivered. He has called the field officer eleven times over six months. Nothing happened. He is being pursued for repayment on an asset he does not have.
people.manner: Angry but controlled. Says the important fact early and plainly if given any opening at all. Repeats it if he is not heard the first time.

people.name: Grace Oyelaran
people.truth: Received the freezer. The business works but she used the first two months of income to buy stock rather than repay, because nobody explained that repayment had already started. She is behind by seven and paying now.
people.manner: Honest about the choice she made. Not defensive about it.

people.name: Yakubu Sani
people.truth: Received the tricycle, it was stolen in month four, he reported it to the police and to our field officer. He has no income from it and no insurance was ever explained to him. He is behind by nine.
people.manner: Flat, resigned. Gives the facts when asked and does not embellish.

participantReport.sharedPicture:
All nine people have answered. People disagree on one thing: Amaka Nwachukwu sees a uniform problem of low revenue across the cohort, but the participants describe a wide range of individual circumstances from success to complete business failure.

Amaka is looking at repayment data. Amaka believes that the businesses are not generating enough revenue to make their payments, and that no other support was part of the loan.

Your goal was to start a grinding business for a steady income. You report that the business is established and the business has a consistent flow of customers.

One colleague sells frozen fish and makes about N30,000 a week. The same colleague missed the first six weeks of payments.

Another colleague is running a transport business with a tricycle. The second colleague says the business is working exactly as the second colleague expected.

A third colleague received a borehole pump to provide clean water. The pump was not installed until the second month, so the third colleague had no income when the first repayments were due.

A fourth colleague was meant to receive a grinding machine. The fourth colleague says the machine was never delivered.

A fifth colleague sells frozen goods. The fifth colleague says nobody told the fifth colleague that repayments would start right away, and the fifth colleague used the first two months of income to buy more stock.

A sixth colleague received a tricycle for a business. The tricycle was stolen, so the sixth colleague has no income from it.

A seventh colleague is running a borehole pump business and now makes about N25,000 a week in sales. The seventh colleague reports that there was not much income for the first three months.

A common experience was a delay between receiving the asset and generating income, which for some resulted in missed payments during the first one to three months. Several businesses are now operating and generating revenue, while others are not.
